sources.entry: 🧰 upgundecha/howtheysre: a curated collection of publicly available resources on SRE at technology and tech-savvy organizations

summary.one_liner: A curated, link-only collection of publicly available SRE resources (blog posts, videos, books, incident reports) from technology companies, grouped by organization.
summary.what_it_does: The README is an awesome-style list rather than a tool. It opens with a topic list (SRE, on-call, incident response and postmortems, monitoring and observability, chaos engineering, platform engineering, and others) and then lists organizations alphabetically, from Achievers to Zomato. Each organization has sub-headings such as Blog Posts, Videos, Books, Major incidents & analysis reports, and Tools, containing titles of external articles and talks. A final "SRECon Mix Playlist" section lists conference videos from various companies. The list links out to external content and contains no code of its own.
use_cases: Finding how companies like Netflix, Google, or GitHub approach site reliability
Researching incident postmortem and blameless review practices
Looking up on-call rotation and alerting case studies
Studying chaos engineering and fault injection examples
Reading public outage and availability reports
Preparing SRE talks or training material from real-world examples
notable: Organized by company, with blog posts, videos, books, and incident reports separated under each organization
Includes GitHub's monthly availability reports from 2020 to 2024 and multiple post-incident analyses
Covers a wide range of SRE topics from monitoring and alerting to chaos engineering and platform engineering
Includes a separate SRECon conference video playlist section
caveats: Contains only links and titles; the README does not include summaries of the linked content
Links are not verified in the README and may go stale over time
README is truncated, so the full list is not visible here
